doc.title: Ray Vega interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, July 20, 2023

title: Chet Baker, wrong notes and overly mathematical young players
summary: Vega discusses Chet Baker's trouble with bridges, seeing Let's Get Lost, what makes a wrong note, and polished but soulless modern playing.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: You know I have to insert because I’ve often asked improvisers about what constitutes a wrong note and most people say there is no wrong note. But you just pointed out something, like Chet never really made the bridge.

He didn’t make the bridge man, I’m sorry. And people are going to hear this and go, “Ray, you’re talking hay.” No this is coming from somebody that absolutely adored Chet Baker’s playing. I will admit that when I saw “Let’s Get Lost” the movie, I had a difficult time listening to Chet’s music for about three years. Because it gave such insight into his personality which for me was like wow this cat was not cool. Such beautiful music coming out of like such a — how shall I say —

Flawed individual. And he was a broken man. He was a broken man. He was broken. And so then my heart, as I get older, goes we are all flawed so don’t judge, Ray. Don’t judge. But I mean I just picked up some recording now, I believe it was in the Netherlands, two sessions of Chet Baker with a quartet in the studio. Beautiful. I buy a lot of Chet. My next dog is going to be called Chet. I’m just kidding. This is Ella by the way. Yes. But so, so the ear is going to let you know. Oh so, wait a minute — what constitutes a wrong note? Well understand something. You’re a half step away from where you need to be. You’re a half step away. You’ve got to know how to resolve what you’re doing. You’ve got to resolve — but Monk, this is the whole thing — the way that jazz is being taught right now it’s so mathematical and I could see it by the performances and the presentations by many of the talented young players that are coming up right now, where their presentation is basically flawless in the way that they execute, the way that they maneuver around chord progressions, the way that they’re able to do all of that stuff is like wow, it’s pristine. But it doesn’t move my soul. That’s me personally. And again I’m

not talking, man, this music is in constant morph so I have to respect whatever the next generation of kids are coming up with. It’s all good. You know? I teach jazz history and — that’s another dog here. Sorry folks. I teach jazz history and I talk about that. I go I’m not in love with everything about it but as a person who plays this music first and foremost, and I don’t consider myself a jazz historian, I consider myself more like a jazz storyteller. You know I’ll share stories. Because I hate, you know the historical end of it can get so boring and so my kids at the school at UVM kind of dig my approach ‘cause I’m coming off from a place like let’s listen to this.
